Why do you think evolution explains what we see in the world?
Science bruh, there's a method to the madness. It's the only way we can actually come close to deriving objective truth about the Universe.

Because the various sciences (cosmology, geology, paleontology, astronomy, biology...) dovetail together perfectly to tell us the history of the world and the universe at large. Biological evolution is underpinned by so many facts and discoveries that it's more well supported than the theory of gravity.
I agree it's a narrative, but I question the merits of it being scientific; what of it has been observed?

Starting at the timeframes - deep time is observed in the universe. You can do this in your driveway with a telescope. Billions of years of cosmic history is established to the naked eye. I personally can see objects that are tens of millions of light years away - the light from those galaxies took that long to get to my telescope.

In paleontology, whole histories of organisms have been reassembled through the fossil record. We can see species develop and lose limbs and functions and become the species we know today. Somewhere around 99% of all species that ever lived on earth are extinct.

In geology, we can see the processes of uplift and erosion that establish long histories on earth. We see layering such as forests, volcanism, oceans, river beds, etc... all layered one on top of another showing vast swaths of time.

In biology, and this is where it gets really exciting, we can see the story of evolution written right inside our own DNA. We have sequenced the DNA of a few hominid species other than our own, and seen how the Neanderthals, Denisovans, and Floriensis represent their own distinct groups... and we can see exactly how much of their unique DNA is in modern Homo Sapien DNA. We can see through molecular clocks, how DNA shows us deep time through the fact that we can sequence it from organisms that lived within the last few hundred thousand years, but since it breaks down beyond that - we can't sequence older DNA from dinosaurs and other animals that lived millions of years ago.

The body of evidence is absolutely astronomical. There is so much, it would take a lifetime to learn all of it.

I appreciate the response; I know it took some time and effort.

So I'm skeptical evolution is an accurate explanation, but to trim down the point to a simple one, it's about limits. The current theory is basically that given enough time and the proper pressures, anything could turn into anything (skipping for now how structures got to be in the first place), and to me that beggars belief. Now I can believe there's variation within kinds (a word I'll use for now instead of species); offspring have differences and similarities with their parents and siblings. But I believe there are limits built-in. I.e. people have been farming for a long time, and when they plant carrots they expect carrots; people have been involved with animal husbandry a long time too, and when people herd cattle, they've been getting cattle as expected as long as this has been going on.

And so I don't think the observed evidence is there for the theory to hold. Bacteria yield bacteria (even after thousands of generations and some slight variations, they're still bacteria), cows yield cows, carrots yield carrots, and so forth. So basically the crux seems to be limits... can a monkey become a man? Can a squirrel become a monkey? Can anything really become anything? I remain skeptical.

You make some excellent point, and hit on the central aspect of evolution - natural selection!

It can't turn anything into anything, but it can turn gnarly purple tubers into long and thin orange carrots; and it can turn wild even toed ungulates into large dumb milk cows - and all in a few thousand years.

And as I mentioned, there is observable proof of deep time and a long established line of evidence of biological evolution throughout.

But the issue really is that if you choose to believe something else, then no evidence will ever be able to convince you. If you are not relying on a method to differentiate fact from fiction, but rather an ideological position that you've chosen, then there's really nothing more to say.

We have the fossil ungulate ancestors of cows. We know how they evolved. We even have the plant fossils that show us how our plants evolved. But there's no use in me showing you if you've already made up your mind.

Google hasn't yielded much results...
Using 17 cubic yards of clay for shooting backfrop

For clay soil, you can figure it will settle into a 45 degree slope. From experience, I'd say the top 1/4 of the pile can be expected to round off and settle.

So, if you want a 6 foot high backstop, start with an 8 foot high pile. Make it as long as you need, and if you have soil left, make it higher. The area of a 90 degree triangle (the two 45 degree sides) is one-quarter the square of the base. For an eight foot pile, the base will be about 11.3 feet, so the area is about 32 square feet, or 3.55 square yards.

So that means for every yard wide your backstop is going to be, you'll need 3.55 cubic yards of clay. That will make a backstop about 4.8 yards wide, which is like 14 feet, which is plenty.

A wise man would double check my math tho. If the angle turns out to be less that 45 degrees you'll get a shorter backstop.

Depending on the clay it could have an angle of repose as low as 25 degrees. What about when it gets wet? That could drop. Maybe you could mix with the soil you already have to get a better material.

Additionally, you have some options to increase the structural properties of the berm. You could also pile it against a wall/support to get more berm height or width. You could also incorporate an internal support structure. Don't forget about geotextiles either.

Some people like to collect their lead for recasting, I'm not sure if that is worth the effort for you, or worth incorporating into your berm design.
